opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Aya was one of the most ambitious things we've tried, and also one of the most chaotic, in the best sense.

The starting point was a gap we kept seeing. Most progress in large language models was concentrated in a handful of languages, mainly English, because that's where the data and the researchers were. If you want to fix that, you can't do it from one lab in one city. The people who know a language best, its idioms and cultural context and what good data even looks like, are spread all over the world. So open science wasn't just a philosophy for Aya. It was the only way the project could work.

Organizing it meant giving up a lot of the control you'd have in a traditional research project. We had thousands of contributors across many countries, many of them not career ML researchers. There were linguists, students, engineers, and native speakers who cared deeply about their language being represented. So a lot of our effort went into building structure that let people contribute meaningfully without needing a PhD or a GPU cluster.

A few things made a real difference. We organized around language ambassadors, people who led and rallied the community for a particular language. That decentralized leadership was critical because no central team could have coordinated that many languages directly. We also built tooling that made contributing straightforward, such as writing, annotating, or improving prompt and completion pairs. Lowering the barrier to entry was probably the most important design decision.

Communication was a big challenge. You're dealing with every time zone, so things had to happen asynchronously. We relied heavily on open channels and regular community calls, and we tried hard to make decisions transparently so people felt ownership rather than feeling like they were doing labor for someone else.

Recognition was another priority. In open science it's easy for contributors to become invisible. We were deliberate about crediting people, including authorship and making clear that this was a collective achievement. I think that's part of why people stayed engaged for so long.

The deeper lesson for me was that the bottleneck in multilingual AI isn't only compute or architecture. It's community, and whose knowledge gets in the room. Aya showed that when you open the door wide enough, people show up, and the resulting data and models reflect a much richer picture of the world than any single lab could produce.

r001.rationale: The response says contributor recognition and authorship credit were deliberate priorities that helped people stay engaged, identifying an incentive change needed to organize the initiative.

r002.rationale: It describes language ambassadors and decentralized leadership, but does not say researchers were organized into small teams.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing to say is that Aya really started from a sense of frustration, honestly. If you look at where most of the progress in large language models was happening, it was overwhelmingly in English and a handful of high-resource languages. And the data that existed for other languages was often machine-translated, low quality, or just didn't exist at all. So the question we asked ourselves was: what would it take to actually close that gap? And the answer was that no single lab could do it. You need people who speak these languages, who understand the cultural context, who can tell you whether an instruction actually makes sense in Swahili or Telugu or Portuguese.

So organizationally, we built it as a very deliberately open, participatory effort. We ended up with around 3,000 collaborators across more than 100 countries, and what I find really interesting is that the participants weren't just researchers in the traditional sense. We had linguists, students, people who were simply fluent speakers and cared deeply about seeing their language represented. And that required us to rethink how we structured the work. You can't run that like a typical research project where everyone's on Slack in the same time zone and has read the same papers.

A few things mattered a lot. One was lowering the barrier to contribution. We built an annotation platform so that someone could contribute instruction-completion pairs or rate quality without needing to know how to fine-tune a model. Another was community infrastructure, having language ambassadors and regional leads who could coordinate locally, run meetups, answer questions in a way that was culturally grounded. And the third, which I think is underappreciated, is giving people real ownership. Contributors are co-authors. Their work is credited. The data and the models are released openly. If you ask people to volunteer their time and expertise, the outputs can't be locked behind an API.

I'd also say we tried to be honest about the trade-offs. Open science at this scale is messy. Quality varies, coordination is hard, and you have to build in a lot of verification and iteration. But I think the payoff is that you end up with something that no closed effort could produce, both in terms of the breadth of languages and in terms of the legitimacy of it. The people the model is meant to serve actually built it. And that's really the model I'd like to see more of in the field, because a lot of the most important problems in AI right now aren't going to be solved by one institution with more compute. They require distributed expertise.

r001.rationale: It says the effort required rethinking how work was structured and emphasizes contributor ownership, co-authorship, and credit as ways to involve collaborators.

r002.rationale: It describes language ambassadors and regional leads, but does not say researchers were organized into small teams.

astra-6.text:
For me, the starting point is that if you want to build something that serves people around the world, you need those people involved in shaping it. That means thinking about participation as more than asking someone to contribute data. It means giving people a voice in what we build, what questions we ask, and how we judge whether we’re making progress.

And organizing that takes a lot of intentional work. You need a shared goal, but you also need smaller, concrete ways for people to contribute. People come with different expertise, different amounts of time, and different perspectives on language. The challenge is creating enough structure that those contributions fit together while leaving room for people to tell you that your assumptions are wrong.

I think that’s a really important part of open science: making the process open, not just the final artifact. You want people to be able to learn from each other, question decisions, and feel ownership of the work. That collaboration is as central to the initiative as the model itself.

r001.rationale: The response calls for intentional participation, shared goals, and open process, but does not identify redesigning collaboration incentives as a requirement.

r002.rationale: It mentions smaller, concrete ways to contribute, but does not say Aya’s researchers are organized into small teams.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the starting point is recognizing that the expertise we need is distributed around the world. If you want to build models that work across languages and cultures, you have to give people from those communities a meaningful role in shaping the work, rather than simply asking them to evaluate something after it’s built.

So with Aya, we’ve tried to organize around a shared goal, while creating different ways for people to contribute. Some people bring research or engineering expertise; others bring deep knowledge of a language and the cultural context around it. The challenge is giving that very diverse group enough structure to collaborate, without assuming that everyone has the same resources or can participate in the same way.

And open science is really about making that process accessible, too. Sharing the resulting artifacts matters, but so does allowing people to understand the decisions, contribute to them, and build on the work. For me, that’s what makes this kind of initiative exciting: you’re expanding who gets to help define what progress looks like.

r001.rationale: The response discusses giving contributors meaningful roles and making participation accessible, but it does not identify redesigning collaboration incentives as a requirement.

r002.rationale: The response describes different ways people contribute and the need for collaboration structure, but it does not say Aya organizes researchers into small teams.
